No, that's not how it works. All of those "left over" addresses (and all the ones you use) are private non-routable addresses. They are useless for most things, except making an outgoing connection with gateway hardware that has to translate addresses AND keep those connections in memory. While you don't want everything to always be available for incoming connections, you DO want to be able to accept incoming connections for certain services or from certain other networks.

I know how it works, I'm pointing out why IPv6 was pushed (it is/was part of the Internet of Things BS). Most homes are running on a 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 on a 255.255.255.0 subnet (or /24). That's 253 addresses available for use in every home with a wireless router. That's more than enough for every home. Now, where there's a chance of running out of IP addresses is on the public side of all those routers as businesses come and go, and new homes are built.

If I setup my router to be 10.0.0.x/8, I'll have 16.8 million IP addresses available for my private personal use. I won't ever approach coming close to running out of IPs on a default home router setups.

It's not a chance of running out. We are out. We ran out years ago. IANA assigned the last of its ranges in 2011. ARIN assigned the last of its delegated ranges in 2015. There are available addresses in ranges in privately assigned pools, but getting them requires negotiating with or purchasing services from the entities that own the assignments.

As far as those private ranges, they break lots of things (not IOT things), and they require more resources on site to manage. Sure you can have a home gateway that can manage a hundred port mappings and translation for a half dozen computers and phones. But the average home gateway doesn't have the memory or cpu cycles to manage thousands of mappings for two hundred chatty devices, and even if they can handle it, they add significant latency. That's not to mention that NAT complicates (requiring smarter and more expensive devices) many protocols like SIP media (VoIP). FTP, DCOM, and referred Kerberos authentication, and completely break many things like IPsec and VPN, and mTLS (protocols that actually provide significant security).

As to IoT devices, a vast majority of them don't even support ipv6 (see the ESP8266: http://bbs.espressif.com/viewtopic.php?t=619)), so the need obviously isn't for them. Even then, small office/home router/gateway/firewall devices wouldn't allow incoming connections by default - the inside device would have to initiate the connection unless the connection is explicitly allowed (which how ipv4 NAT winds up working in effect any way). Almost all IoT devices work by making an outgoing connection to a central management service.

What he is showing is not, per se, an objectively "easy" type of painting. Its just easier for a lot of people to start this style out than some other forms of art. In other words, its more accessible to people without any experience than other styles.

He is keeping actual technique rather simple, and the simplicity isn't even the important part, just uniform across landscapes. Using a single technique to accomplish as much as possible within the same painting, so you can get more done learning less. To keep newer people interested. And though it isn't acknowledged often, simple things don't always translate to "easy". Bob Ross' style was about simplicity of form (using the smallest number of strokes to make an object recognizable) and, whenever possible, using strokes to which the tools lend themselves naturally. It bears some fundamental similarity to speed painting, though obviously the two are not interchangeable.

With that in mind, the most pleasing parts of your painting (in my opinion) are the areas where you let that philosophy take the reigns (like the knife work at the edges of the stream, or the quick, overlapping strokes on the left midground), while the areas that seem out of place (the center of the stream foreground, or the bank to the right of it) appear to be areas where you got in close and applied fine motor work. Neither one is a bad thing, mind you. Both techniques can harmonize in one painting with the right composition and blending choices. But if you're trying to paint in the style of Bob Ross you'll want to do more of the former and less of the latter.

That said this is really excellent work for a beginner, and as cool as it is to watch Bob Ross pass a knife over a paint smear and make a cabin appear, you clearly have the talent to effectively experiment with a variety of techniques before you focus on his in particular. Knowing what you don't like is just as important as knowing what you do, at lest where creative endeavors are concerned.
